We picked Woburn Forest, which is the most modern centre parks in the UK and represents their current best thinking, presumably, on how to build a centre parks. We are also interested in going to a few of their older ones to see how maintenance has been over the years and where their original ideas evolved from.

Booking Experience

First off the booking experience when you go onto the page looks like you're booking an airline ticket. If you have visited before you are signing in at this point

Note the ability to chat with someone at any point.

![][image1]

The options to purchase are either Monday to Friday(4 nights) or Friday to Monday(3 nights). Or Monday to Monday(7 nights) or Friday to Friday(7 nights). There is no I would like this day or that day. You fit within their schedule rather than vice versa.

There are options in the booking process to bring a dog for an extra fee. Presumably they also have rules associated with bringing a dog (research). And they also have the ability to provide disability lodges (research) free of charge.

You can choose how many beds you need for the number of people. And you can choose the number of lodges that you need at this stage. Note they use the word lodge rather than Semi-detached bungalow.

If you want to book more than three lodges, you need to call a phone number. I don't understand why they're doing this, but presumably there's a reason. (Research)

For Monday to Friday (4 nights), this was the price when we wanted to go.

![][image2]

For Friday to Monday (3 nights) this was the price when we wanted to go.

![][image3]

For the woodland lodge during the four nights midweek they are selling at 144 pounds a night and For the three nights over the weekend, they are selling at £259 a night. This represents an 80% premium for the weekend nights, over the weekday nights.

![][image4]

If you book a full week at the same time we're going, it would appear to be 300 pounds more expensive than booking four days, four nights, and three nights separately. Which doesn't make any sense to me at all. (research and double triple check)

If we were to book this trip in mid-August rather than early June, we are looking at the price being 2.4 times as much, or an increase of 140%. Center parks are famous for having dynamic pricing Presumably they do special offers if things are available and they don't have occupancy at the last moment. (research)

It's also worth noting that part of their business model is to charge for the apartment, regardless of the number of people that stay in it, as long as it's within the occupancy limits prescribed. This way, rather than selling per bed, they're selling per home and they incentivise people to fill up their lodges, which in turn drives additional revenue through the activity half of the revenue account.

They have two basic types of lodge in a two-bedroom and three-bedroom format. All lodges come with a log burner. The basic ones, all lodges are en suite. All lodges are accessed from between 3 and 4pm. The slightly posher lodges being accessed at 3, the cheaper ones being accessed at 4\. 

For a lodge with a hot tub and sauna, they essentially charge double, which seems to me to be extremely high margin. They've probably added $10,000 of additional cost to the lodge, which probably in Kenyan money might cost $60,000. And then they're now booking that out at double the price. At the time of booking, they only had six left. There's that scarcity thing they have going on with the hot tub and the sauna. I have seen a friend do this with a little hut in a field on his farm in the UK and by adding a hot tub he's been able to charge £200 a night for a shepherd's hut. 

This upselling around the core product is absolutely crucial to how Centre Parks works. And they've made it very frictionless from what I understand. The more we see of this, the more I will comment on it. A good analogy might be the Muthaiga Club where it's very frictionless to spend money in the Muthaiga Club.

![][image5]

They also have a handful of bigger lodges, four and six bedroom, which are larger, maybe double families, families with grandparents, that kind of situation. Composite families, families with lots of children could book out. But they've seemed to have created scarcity in those. Many of these were fully booked at the time of booking for us when we were booking two and a half months in advance. 

![][image6]![][image7]

![][image8]![][image9]

![][image10]![][image11]

![][image12]

This is the Forest Lodge priced at a modest 12% premium. The forest lodge appears to be slightly bigger and I'm not 100% sure but it might be detached. (Research) It also had a bath which they called a hydro bath. This naming things in a sexy way is another thing I see with center parks. We're going to stay in lodges not bungalows\!

Below are the photos of the woodland lodge, which, like I say above, were slightly cheaper than the forest lodge. Unfortunately, a floor plan was not available on the website.

![][image13]![][image14]

![][image15]![][image16]

![][image17]

There's also the ability to virtually walk around the lodge that you're going to stay in. This made me feel pretty comfortable with the product I was going to receive For my stay.

![][image18]

I booked the cheaper one. We need to research the ratio of cheaper ones to expensive ones. (research)

After choosing the lodge that I wanted from an option of about six you really start to see the upselling process begin.

![][image19]![][image20]

Notice here how they don't have a cheaper and a more expensive alternative. They have you don't get any choice and you don't pay anything or you choose and you pay something. I went for the lucky dip and asked them to choose for us and saved money. But if this was the second time I was staying and I actually knew the benefits of staying in different places, I would probably pay extra to be in the exact place I wanted to be. Note that a very high number of people using Centre Parks return again within three or four years. (research)

![][image21]

If you wanted to go further and choose the exact launch you wanted, you pay another £40. I didn't do this. But you see this process of upselling in action again.

Having chosen the lodge, we move on to More upselling where they're selling us the “little extras”.

![][image22]

If you want to access your lodge two hours earlier, you can pay £65. 

![][image23]

The way people get around center parks is often bicycles. You can bring your own, but this is obviously a logistical exercise for a family. Or you can just hire theirs. And you see how they point out that you probably need it anyway. And you can hire it when you're there, but it's going to be more expensive than if you hire it now. A bit like an airline and extra luggage. We paid for this. Cost us an additional £84.

![][image24]

Fire logs. Okay, we bought these. You notice how we're gonna be staying four nights but they sell us a package of three. So if you want to fire every night, you've got to buy six. I don't know if this is intentional, but the cynic in me thinks it might be. We bought two packs of three.

![][image25]

Gyms are notorious for people not using them. I have a gym membership and don't use it. Jason uses his religiously. But in reality most people are more like me. All the same, I think that it was cheap, so I got two of them.

![][image26]

I mean, who doesn't want a barbecue on a family holiday?

![][image27]

![][image28]

I didn't get the starter pack, but it was a good way of gently reminding me that I'm booking an accommodation without food, toiletries, Washing up liquid. etc.and that I should either buy food there or bring my own. 

![][image29]

There was also a larger family grocery pack to get you started. My plan is to go to a supermarket, stock up and then head to Centre Parks With all the stuff we will need For four days. I understand there is a mini supermarket in the centre parks which is very expensive. When we go there we will do some price comparison on some basic items between the mini supermarket and a normal supermarket in the UK. (research)

![][image30]

And finally, a nice touch If you would like to support a children's charity, you can From as little as one pound.

![][image31]

The little extras quickly added up and ended up adding £157 to the accommodation fee. This was 27% additional revenue. Had we been a family rather than just myself and Jason I can easily imagine that we would have hired four or five bikes. I look forward to seeing the type of bikes that Centre Parks has developed for low maintenance and easy security and identification. (research)

![][image32]

At this stage, if you have booked before with them, entering your details presumably becomes seamless. You could have logged on earlier in the process, but this is the point at which existing customers' lives get made a little bit easier.

![][image33]

I'm not sure why they ask these questions, but I will think about it. And I'm sure there's some logic to this because it's the only personal question they've asked, or questionnaire-type question So presumably this is very important to them. (think / Research)

![][image34]

They are going to send me a traditional old-fashioned welcome pack in the mail. I'm fascinated\! I will add to this when I get to my parents and check it out. (research)

![][image35]

I will remain signed in for the next six months. I understand I will be coming back to the webpage quite a bit in the weeks and months before my trip to plan my activities. From what I understand, their marketing through emails is going to start encouraging me to do this from the point I booked the trip. Let's see.

![][image36]

A clever way to get you signed up to their news and marketing. And also reward you next time you come, which I'm sure they will be reminding me about after I've taken my first trip. I don't know what Aquasana Forest Spa is, but presumably it's a little bit like Center Parks, but for spas. 

I have literally never felt the need or wish to sign up to somebody's marketing email list before. 50 quid off my next break sounds like a reasonable deal to me. Obviously for research purposes I'm signing up anyway, but this is just an observation.

![][image37]

Jason Now also gets his own email address added so that he can log on and start booking his own activities before he arrives too. Note the disclaimer where I'm sharing Jason's personal information with them. Not totally sure this would be legal in Kenya. (research)

![][image38]

Next, they ask how many cars you're bringing. This means they don't get into a situation where they don't have enough car parking spaces. I'm not sure if this would be needed in Kenya. \-But I can see the advantage of having those number plates put into a digital system, you then simply arrive at a security gate, it reading your number plate and lets you into the resort. A bit like happens with the parking lots in village market and places like that once you've paid. This would be a pretty posh arrival experience.

![][image39]

At this point, if you have a discount code or a repeat guest offer, you can enter it into the system and receive a discount. 

Also, you can ensure your booking such that you can cancel or amend for free. I don't know what the statutory rights of somebody booking a hotel in Kenya would be in terms of cancelling their booking. Frankly, it didn't offer all the information I was expecting here. Like, how far before you travel can you... cancel your booking? I presume it's all in the terms and conditions. I didn't pay for this. Presumably, this can be simply a product from an insurance company or the centre parcs itself can essentially turn this fee into an insurance pot to cover cancellations And adjust the fee over time to reflect the reality and the mathematics of cancellations.

![][image40]

Before I proceed and book it, they warn me and give me more information, which I felt had been lacking previously about this insurance policy. Again, upselling in action. Note the green button and the yes to buy it and the slightly anonymous button to not add this additional fee.

![][image41]

![][image42]

![][image43]

The second that you've booked your accommodation, they're now into the process of upselling you activities. There's also some administrative stuff like the accessibility form in case you come with disabilities. There's a section explaining what's included. The large groups form. You can click through to your booking overview at any time to see what you've booked so far. A bit like an airline you can check in before arrival. That seems like it'll get you through security much quicker. There's some fear of missing out here with booking activities.

I also received an email giving me directions to the holiday resort, obviously confirming my booking and what I paid for in invoice form, giving me the ability to amend something that's not right if you've got a concern, basically a sort of helpline and reiterating the disability needs and starting the process of saying, "Come on, start booking your activities."

At this stage they are also pushing me to download the app To book activities on.

![][image44]

The app has received over 100,000 downloads and has a rating of 4.9 on the App Store. This was an innovation that happened relatively recently in Centre Park's history and has proved to be a huge success apparently.

It wanted quite a lot of notification rights on my phone, something I really don't like, but I did it In the interests of research, I'm not sure I would have done it otherwise. But I guess everyone's different on this.

![][image45]

That is the Schedule of activities that I booked for the week. The restaurants I didn’t pay for, I simply made bookings. The way I understand it, I can cancel any of these things 24 hours beforehand and get my money back. Maybe perhaps that’s 12 hours. As you can see, the activities, although I maybe went a little bit over the top, come to a similar amount of money to the housing that I booked. I looked into the activities and it’s clear that some of these things are available all the time. And some of these things appear to be on a sort of rotating schedule. So presumably the staff that manage, for instance, the outdoor archery also maybe manage the clay pigeon shooting or the… the junior archery. 

Something that is well documented about Centre Parks is the fact that they create a situation of artificial scarcity within their park. So that if you don’t book ahead of time, you can easily find yourself in a situation where you can’t access activities or dinners and things like that while you’re there. It will be interesting to see if we can book things while we are there, or that scarcity really does become apparent as we get closer to the time. 

Two areas that we definitely have to research further at this stage are the scheduling of activities and the scarcity idea, just how far they have taken that. So I will be getting a ratio of tables to guests in the park for the restaurants. But also trying to maybe work out the total number of activities that are available at any one time in the park. 

I haven’t put it in our schedule, but you can see on Tuesday morning we have lots of time at the beginning to go to the water park and enjoy the water park. The water park is considered the cornerstone of the entire park. Because it is indoors, it means that you can use this swimming pool all year round in bad weather in the UK. This in the UK, as you can imagine, is particularly exciting to customers. I wonder if we could have anything like the same effect with our water park in kenya. I suppose not, but we could heat it. 

It should be noted that I have specifically not done any of the children’s stuff because it was only me and Jason there. This is also an area that would need more research. 

I think something else that I’ve realised is these parks tend to have a large lake as well as a swimming pool, and the lake is used for additional water activities. 

All in all, I found the activity booking quite simple, although I did need to write down, in a little table form, on a scrap piece of paper, my activities as I booked them, so as not to overlap or have big gaps where I didn’t want the gaps. So I felt that the system could have been cleaner. One of the things that I worry about with this idea of booking your activities at certain times is Kenyan’s ability to be late for things and the amount of customer dissatisfaction that this could easily create if we strictly follow English timekeeping.

We have booked £430 of activities against £730 of accommodation at this stage. I think it’s very possible we can add another £200 in food spend when we are there, meaning that we’re probably sort of 80 or 90% of our accommodation spend in activities. I would say that because we’re doing this to study the business, I might have booked us more than I would have done otherwise. 

Some anxiety that I might have before arriving I wish I’d booked in so I could get my house two hours earlier and I didn’t and now I can’t find a way to do it online so if we arrive anytime too far before the time we’re meant to arrive on Monday I don’t know where we would put all our suitcases because we haven’t come with the car. Anyway, just a thought there. 

This is a really thorough pre-visit analysis, John — you've clearly got a sharp eye for the upselling mechanics and pricing architecture. Let me flag some areas you might want to pay attention to during the visit that aren't yet covered, particularly through the UHC lens.

**Operational and physical design observations to make on-site:**

The document is heavily focused on the digital booking journey (which is excellent), but once you're physically there, you'll want to look at how the "closed ecosystem" actually works in practice. Specifically: how do they handle the transition from car park to lodge? What's the vehicle policy once you're inside — are cars restricted to arrival/departure only, with internal movement by foot and bike? This has big implications for Kikampala's site planning and the sense of escape you want to create.

Pay close attention to **wayfinding and signage** throughout the resort. How do guests navigate between their lodge, the waterpark, restaurants, and activities? Is it intuitive or do people rely entirely on the app? The physical environment design is something you can't replicate from a website.

**Staff interaction model** is another gap. You've captured the digital touchpoints brilliantly, but watch carefully how staff engage with guests. Are they proactive or reactive? What's the ratio of staff to guests at different touchpoints? How are activity instructors managed between rotations (you've started noting this with the archery/clay pigeon observation — keep pulling that thread)? For UHC's ethical positioning, the quality of human interaction will be a major differentiator in the Kenyan context where hospitality warmth is a genuine cultural asset.

**Revenue capture mechanics on-site** deserve close attention beyond what you've pre-booked. How frictionless is spending money once you're there? You've mentioned the Muthaiga Club analogy — look at whether they use wristbands, the app, cards, or some combination. This maps directly to your Club Account and how you'll design the on-property payment experience. Watch what happens when someone wants to do a spontaneous activity versus a pre-booked one — that's where you'll see the scarcity model in real time.

**A few specific things I'd add to your research list:**

The **maintenance and wear observation** is mentioned briefly (wanting to visit older parks), but while you're at Woburn, look carefully at how units age. Check the skirting boards, the shower seals, the kitchen drawer runners, the decking outside. These are the things that tell you whether a property feels five years old or fifteen. This feeds directly into your refurbishment clause (Section 9\) and whether four weeks of annual maintenance is realistic for Kenyan coastal conditions with salt air and humidity.

You haven't mentioned **noise and privacy between units**. For your semi-detached units at Kikampala, this is critical. Listen for neighbours. Check wall thickness. This will be one of the first complaints if you get it wrong, and it's much harder to fix retrospectively.

**Food and beverage** gets only a passing mention. This is likely 20-30% of on-site revenue for Center Parcs. Map the full F\&B offering: how many restaurants, what cuisine variety, price points, whether there's a grab-and-go option, how the on-site mini-market is positioned relative to the restaurants. Your note about price-comparing the mini-market with a normal supermarket is good — also check whether they stock basics that people forget (phone chargers, sunscreen, kids' medicines) at premium prices.

**Check-out process and departure experience** — you've got detailed notes on arrival but nothing about how they handle departure. Is there a property inspection? How do they handle the damage deposit or condition report? This is directly relevant to your clause 12.3 (property condition report on the first day of arrival).

**Children's programming** — you've flagged this as a gap, which is good since you've already designed three age-based streams for UHC. While you're there, even without kids, walk through the kids' zones. Look at the physical safety measures, the ratio of supervisors, the registration process, and critically, how parents are freed up to do adult activities while kids are engaged. That's the real value proposition for families.

Finally, one strategic observation: your note about **Kenyan timekeeping versus English timekeeping** for activity scheduling is really important and deserves more than a passing mention. This could fundamentally affect how you design your booking and activity management system. Center Parcs can run tight 45-minute activity slots because British culture supports that. You may need to build in more buffer time, or design activities that are more flexible in duration. Worth discussing with your partner on the trip.
